poiBMK-desc:
West Africa suffered some of the continent's worst damage in the Great Mistake, and when the Congo Crisis tore the African Union apart, {{poiBMK001|it was cut off from the rest of the continent}} and left to fend for itself. Nigeria, Cameroon, Niger and Chad broke apart, and from their pieces and the old states of the coast and the Sahel came a crowd of successors, many of them poor, some of them failed, all of them alone.

The Bamako Compact is their answer. Signed in the capital of the Mali Federation, it joins Mauritania, the Mali Federation, Burkina Faso, Ghana, Liberia, the Ivory Coast, {{poiBMK006|Benin}}, {{poiBMK004|Sokoto}}, {{poiBMK003|Biafra}}, {{poiBMK005|Adamawa}}, Mboumo, Ogowe, Kanem and Tsade in a bloc that stretches from the Atlantic to Lake Chad. Its members keep their sovereignty, coordinate their defence, and present one face to the great powers around them: the East African Federation to the east, which dreams of a single Pan-African nation, and the Kimpwanza League to the south.

The Compact is rich in what the world needs to rebuild: iron from Mauritania, Liberia and Burkina, manganese and bauxite from Ghana and Ogowe, oil and gas from Biafra and Sokoto, and lithium from Mali. Much of that wealth flows through one company. Morgan Industries propped up Biafra, has bought its way into Benin and Adamawa, and would like nothing better than to own the rest. Morgan's largest client state and its fiercest enemy sit at the same table in Bamako, and every member knows it.
poiBMK001-desc:
When the Congo Crisis struck in 2134, the African Union lost West Africa almost overnight. Its units in the region were stranded, cut off from supply, and many were never seen again. The governments they left behind had already been failing. The ineffectual Union had floundered in its attempts to keep order after the Great Mistake, and it could not stop the breakup of Nigeria, Cameroon and many other nations.

What followed was a long century of improvisation. Where the nations of West Africa were not stifled under oppressive governments, they were terrorised by warlords. The East African Federation has kept up some contact with North Africa over the decades, but West Africa has remained a world apart from it, a region of small states that learned to survive without anyone's help and have little intention of asking for it now.
poiBMK002-desc:
Nwabudike Morgan is self-confident to the point of arrogance. To him life is a game of status measured by economic success, and he loves the game for its own sake. He has few ethical values beyond the acquisition of wealth, though he believes in the fulfilment of contracts, and once he gives his word it can be relied on. He believes any interaction can be controlled with the right inducement: money, affection or the threat of harm. He presents himself as an affable businessman willing to work for anyone, but in the end he means to go from merchant prince to emperor.

Born in 2145 to an old noble family tied to the royalty of former Nigeria, he built a world-class business empire from the ground up. Family seed money went into the arms trade during the collapse of the African Union, the profits paid for a mercenary force that helped the young Biafran government during the breakup of Nigeria, and the reward was control of many of Biafra's key industries. By the early 2190s Morgan Industries spanned mercenary companies, media outlets, agribusiness, food transport and food brokering, and the Morgan SafeHaven Hotel Fortress chain for the discriminating executive.

Not every venture has paid off. An eager push into the Sokoto market ended when the pro-Morgan government there was overthrown by a motley coalition of eco-Islamist communalists, and a hostile takeover attempt afterwards failed outright. His expansions into Benin and Adamawa face growing public scrutiny, as nationalists fear what will become of their countries under his influence. His shareholders are restless. Something will have to give, and they will want their cut whatever happens.
poiBMK003-desc:
Biafra was fortunate, in many ways. It emerged from the breakup of Nigeria quickly and organised well, not least thanks to Morgan Industries, whose mercenaries defended the young government and whose money rebuilt its industries. Within a decade it had become a beacon of comparative stability in the region, and it remains the Compact's richest member.

The price is that Biafra is less and less its own. Morgan Industries controls many of its key industries, and its state-run corporations are being absorbed one by one into Morgan's portfolio. When the old railway station at Kano was replaced by a gleaming new maglev hub, it was Morgan who cut the ribbon, to the applause of workers who had been left unemployed by the government before him. Morgan makes no secret that he expects the Biafran government itself to follow, and few Biafrans seem to mind.
poiBMK004-desc:
Sokoto also rose from the ashes of Nigeria, absorbing a few statelets that survived the collapse of Niger and Chad. It never found its feet. Poverty and violence ran rife, its young government proved incapable of keeping order, and the country came to resemble a collection of survivalist communities more than a functioning nation.

Morgan Industries saw opportunity in Biafra's northern neighbour and made overtures to its government. The government accepted. Its people did not. The pro-Morgan regime was overthrown by a motley coalition of eco-Islamist communalists, and Morgan's attempt at a hostile takeover afterwards ended in defeat. Sokoto is now the Compact's loudest voice against corporate influence, and a standing embarrassment in Morgan's boardroom.
poiBMK005-desc:
Adamawa was devastated by three blows in a row: the Great Mistake, the breakup of Nigeria and Cameroon, and the collapse of the African Union. After a brief rally when it won nationhood, it fell into famine and decline, a textbook example of a failed state.

Morgan Industries brought investment and capital, and turned its farms into an agricultural powerhouse. Crop yields are up, desertification is in retreat and starvation is receding. Morgan also owns a controlling share of the country's land and resources. Automation has left many farmworkers jobless, new factories have only partly absorbed them, and resentment at Biafrans coming to dominate the economy has turned to protests, blockades and a wave of bombings against Morgan's assets. Morgan Security has been kept busy.
poiBMK006-desc:
Benin is where Morgan Industries is testing its future. The company is negotiating the handover of the country's public services, and its board sees no reason a government should do anything a company can do better. Many Beninese are slow to trust the message, and the question of who will pay for health care once the private clinics move in remains unanswered.

The negotiations are led by Tejumola-Maduka, {{poiBMK002|Nwabudike Morgan}}'s favourite nephew, known to everyone as T.M. A beloved public figure, married into the Reilly Heavy Industries fortune and increasingly active in philanthropy and politics, he shares his uncle's drive but not his faith in capital. He has seen what men with Morgan's beliefs did to Africa and the world, and after the disaster in Sokoto, he fears history repeating itself. He is influential, but not even a member of the board, and his uncle's word is all but absolute within the company.
